Financial and Estate Planning Literacy: Item Validation and Categorical CFA

Restricted to participants who reported being 35 or older

Author

Jamie C. Lee

Published

August 27, 2026

Summary

ImportantAge-restricted sample

This document is a re-run of ep_literacy_analysis.qmd on participants who reported being 35 years of age or older. Age is taken from the self-reported band item (age), not from Prolific’s recorded age (p_age), so a participant is retained if they selected 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, 65-74, 75+.

Of the 399 participants in the raw file, 116 reported an age band below 35 and 1 gave no usable reported age (“prefer not to answer” or blank); both groups are dropped, leaving 282. The restriction is applied before the bot-detection flags, so every N in this document — including the “full” N in Section 1 — refers to the 35+ sample.

Everything else about the analyses is unchanged. The restriction removes 29% of the raw sample, so numbers throughout will differ from the all-ages document, and any comparison involving age operates over a truncated range.

In this document, we perform a set of analyses that test whether estate planning literacy (EPL) is an empirically distinct construct from financial literacy (FL) (Fernandes et al. 2014).

Document Outline

Section Details
1. Bot exclusion checks Applies the two bot-detection rules (from Zhang et al.’s user package) and defines the analytic sample. This is the only section that uses the full 35+ N = 282. Everything from Section 2 onward uses the post-exclusion sample of N = 268.

6. Question 2 Does each factor measure something meaningful on their own? Two items can correlate because both tap a general literacy factor or because both tap a more narrow construct (e.g., financial literacy); a bifactor model separates the two and asks whether anything coherent is left inside each sub-factor once the general factor is accounted for.
7. Reconciling results from Sections 5 and 6 Why “the three-factor model fits best” and “most variance is general literacy” results are not contradictory.
8. Association with EP engagement Whether having done estate planning is related to EPL over and above financial literacy. Reported as partial correlations rather than regressions, because the causal direction is ambiguous.
9. Exploratory analyses Four further measures: behavioural expectations among participants who have not yet done anything, self-reported prior exposure to the FL items, superstition, and the Death Attitude Profile-Revised.

NoteNote

fin_8 is dropped from the analyses: I tried different ways of coding the correct response, but none of them discriminated between high and low scorers. All analyses reported in this document include only the 12 FL items and 12 EPL items, 24 total.

0.0.1 Overview of Results

Question 1 — do the items map onto distinguishable factors? (Section 5) Yes. A two-factor model that separates financial literacy (FL) from estate planning literacy (EPL) fits significantly better than a one-factor general-literacy model (scaled \(\Delta\chi^2\)(1) = 19.2, p < .001). Splitting EPL further into financial-consequence and legal/administrative dimensions improves fit again (scaled \(\Delta\chi^2\)(2) = 14.4, p < .001). Of the models evaluated, the three-factor model fits best (CFI = 0.971, RMSEA = 0.023). Therefore, the three content domains are empirically distinguishable: treating all 24 items as indicators of a single undifferentiated factor misses meaningful structure in the data.

Question 2 — do the blocks measure distinct abilities of their own? (Section 6) Not necessarily. Although the three factors are distinguishable, they are also strongly correlated (0.63–0.82). The better fit of the three-factor model tells us that items within the same domain share additional covariance, but it does not tell us whether that covariance reflects a substantial domain-specific ability or is mostly part of a broader ability shared across all items.

A bifactor model separates these two sources of variance. It estimates a general (literacy) factor shared by all 24 items while simultaneously asking whether items within FL, EPL-Fin, and EPL-Legal still share meaningful variance after that general factor is accounted for. Most of the common variance is attributable to the general factor. FL and EPL-Legal retain only modest domain-specific variance, while EPL-Fin retains essentially none: its specific factor cannot be estimated reliably, indicating that the three EPL-Fin items cohere primarily because of what they share with the broader general factor rather than because they measure a distinct EPL-Fin ability.

Practical upshot. The results support retaining the three-factor structure as the best description of the item covariance, but they provide much weaker support for interpreting the three domains as separate, reliable subscales. The measure is therefore best scored primarily with a total score rather than separate subscores. The three-item EPL-Fin subscale, in particular, should not be interpreted on its own.

Does the Age Cut-off Change the Answers?

Mostly no. Section 10 refits the central analyses at three nested cut-offs — all ages (n = 372), 25+ (n = 329), and 35+ (n = 268) — and what follows is a condensed summary of what it finds. Figures below are given in that order, all ages / 25+ / 35+. Because the samples are nested rather than independent, the point of the comparison is whether a conclusion survives, not whether three separate estimates agree.

What does not change. Both model comparisons are significant at every cut-off (2-factor over 1-factor, scaled \(\chi^2\) = 33.6 / 22.2 / 19.2; 3-factor over 2-factor, 20.7 / 16.9 / 14.4; all p < .001), the three-factor model keeps the best fit (CFI = 0.966 / 0.965 / 0.971), and the EPL-Fin specific factor is unidentified in all three. On the validity side, the partial correlation between EP engagement and EPL net of financial literacy holds throughout (0.215 (< .001) / 0.195 (< .001) / 0.198 (0.001)), while the reverse partial — FL net of EPL — stays indistinguishable from zero throughout (0.028 (0.591) / 0.042 (0.446) / 0.040 (0.513)). Total-scale reliability barely moves (alpha = 0.816 / 0.808 / 0.806). Everything the document concludes in Sections 5, 6, and 8 is unaffected by where the age cut-off is drawn.

What does change. Two statistics, and both should be read as cautions rather than as findings about older people:

  • The zero-order EPL-versus-FL comparison (Steiger’s test: +0.104 (0.036) / +0.083 (0.108) / +0.088 (0.134)) is significant only in the full sample. It fails already at 25+, so this is not an effect of restricting to 35+ — it is simply the most marginal test in the document, and it should not carry the comparative claim when the partial correlations above are stable.
  • The FL specific factor (omega-HS = 0.323 / 0.254 / 0.080) is largely unchanged from all ages to 25+ and then drops sharply at 35+. Resampling indicates the index is unstable at these sample sizes, so this is most likely estimation noise rather than a real age difference. See Section 10 for the full argument.

One consistent trend. EPL-Fin gets weaker as the cut-off rises — its alpha falls (0.599 / 0.566 / 0.529) while its correlation with financial literacy rises. This runs in the same direction at both cut-offs and strengthens, rather than qualifies, the recommendation in Section 11.1 to rebuild that block.

1 Bot Exclusion Checks

Two behavioral indicators, both adapted from Zhang et al., are used to exclude potential bots.

1.1 The Two Detectors

Prompt injection. Participants select the apple juice brands they buy regularly. Hidden within the response-option text is an instruction, displayed in white font against a white background, directing participants to select “Golden Grove” - a fictitious brand. Because the instruction is visually undetectable to a human respondent, human participants would not be expected to follow it.

Reverse shibboleth. Participants estimated the calories, carbohydrates, fat, and protein in an 8-oz glass of apple juice without looking up the information. Individuals are flagged as potential bots if they demonstrate “superhuman knowledge,” which is defined as having all four of their responses fall within a small range around the true values: 105–120 cal, 26–29 g carbs, 0–0.5 g fat, 0–1 g protein.

Fat and protein are relatively easy to get correct, because both true values sit near zero and “0” is a common lay-guess. Calories and carbohydrates are more the discriminating items.

1.2 Validation Checks on the Bot Detection Measures

Survey-taking bots may vary considerably in sophistication. At one extreme, simple bots may respond randomly or according to basic rules, producing low-quality or internally inconsistent answers. At the other extreme, more sophisticated bots may use large language models or other generative AI tools to produce responses that resemble those of attentive human participants. Intermediate cases may rely on scripted heuristics, patterned responding, or selective use of automated tools.

If these different forms of automation are present in our sample, bot responses may appear at both extremes of performance on the literacy items: unsophisticated bots may perform unusually poorly (if they are responding randomly), whereas more sophisticated AI-assisted bots may perform unusually well. The exclusion patterns reported below are consistent with this possibility, though they do not by themselves establish that flagged responses were generated by bots.

Detector Top band Everyone else Odds ratio 95% CI p

The flag rate is 0.0–4.8% across the bottom four bands and 38.1% in the top band. Of the 14 excluded participants, 8 had a perfect EPL score — 57% of all exclusions, against a 6.4% base rate. The EPL ceiling bar falls from 18 to 10 while its neighbour barely moves.

Interestingly, nearly all of this signal is driven by the reverse-shibboleth measure (OR = 99, compared with 7.0 for prompt injection, which flags only 3 participants). In other words, one detector is doing most of the work. This raises the question of whether the prompt-injection measure contributes enough meaningful information to justify its use in future studies.

WarningControlling for age

Inheritors are on average 7.9 years older than non-inheritors (59.1 vs 51.2). Inheriting is also related to age. Adjusting for age shrinks the effect but does not remove it — inheritance is still worth +0.99 EPL points (p = 0.005) with age held constant.

3 Measures and Scoring

12 financial literacy items (from Fernandes et al., 2014) and 12 estate planning literacy items (self-generated). The EPL items split by content: ep_1–ep_9 concern what a legal instrument does or who holds legal authority (intestacy, beneficiary designations, right of survivorship, powers of attorney, trust funding, guardianship); ep_10–ep_12 concern the monetary consequences of an estate’s composition (debt satisfaction, illiquidity, net vs. gross value).

Item-rest r is the point-biserial correlation between the item (scored 0/1) and the summed score on the remaining items in its own block, with the item itself excluded. Standardized loadings come from the three-factor model in Section 5.

The items provide fairly good coverage across levels of difficulty, as reflected in the proportion of participants who answered each item correctly.

EPL items elicit substantially more “I don’t know” responses than FL items (10.4% vs 6.5% on average), consistent with participants having less familiarity or prior exposure to estate-planning knowledge.

4.1 Item-Rest Correlation

The pass rate describes how difficult an item is. The item-rest correlation describes how well the item discriminates — whether the people who do well on the rest of the scale are also the people who get this item right.

It is computed by scoring the item 0/1, summing each participant’s score on all the other items in that item’s own block, and correlating the two.

How to interpret the values:

Item-rest r Reading
≥ .30 Conventionally adequate. High scorers reliably get it right.
.20–.30 Weak but usable, especially for a very easy or very hard item.
0–.20 Contributes little. The item is close to unrelated to the rest of the scale.
≤ 0 Red flag. People who do well elsewhere tend to get this item wrong — usually a miskeyed answer, ambiguous wording, or an item measuring something else entirely.
WarningVery easy and very hard items are mechanically penalized

If 95% of people answer an item correctly there is almost no variance left for it to correlate with anything, so a modest item-rest r on an extreme item is not by itself evidence of a bad item.

In this instrument every item-rest correlation is positive, ranging from 0.21 to 0.53. No item behaves in reverse, which is the failure mode that matters most.

4.3 The Correlation Structure Behind the Models

I report tetrachoric correlations to assess whether the items are meaningfully related while remaining sufficiently distinct from one another (i.e., no correlations approaching 0.90).

What to look for. If the three sets of items reflect three distinct factors, then the diagonal blocks of the correlation matrix below (which show correlations among items within the same factor) should appear darker than the off-diagonal blocks (which show correlations among items across factors).

Table 14. Mean Tetrachoric Correlation Within and Between Blocks
FL EPL-Fin EPL-Legal
FL 0.379 0.344 0.196
EPL-Fin 0.344 0.434 0.250
EPL-Legal 0.196 0.250 0.260
Diagonal cells are the mean correlation among items within a block; off-diagonal cells are the mean correlation between items of different blocks.

Reading the pattern. Items do cohere more with their own block than with others — mean within-block r = 0.36 versus between-block r = 0.26. That gap is what Question 1 detects as distinguishable factors. But notice how modest it is, and notice two specific cells:

  • FL with EPL-Fin (0.34) is almost as high as FL with itself (0.38). The EPL-Fin items are nearly as related to the financial literacy items as the financial literacy items are to each other. This is the same finding that recurs throughout the document, visible here in the raw correlations before any model is fitted.
  • EPL-Legal with itself (0.26) is barely above EPL-Legal with EPL-Fin (0.25).

The other thing to notice is what the whole matrix looks like: almost every cell is positive and moderate, averaging at 0.28. Most items are positively related to nearly every other item, even when compared to items that belong to a different factor.

This figure foreshadows both answers to come: there exists a multi-factor structure (Question 1 — the factors are distinguishable), but there seems to be a general factor too (Question 2 — the strong correlations between the factors reflects a broader ability shared across all items).

5 Question 1: Do the items load onto a single “general literacy factor or distinct factors?

The first question is whether financial literacy and estate planning literacy are separate things at all, and whether EPL itself splits in two factors. We answer this question by testing the fit of three latent models.

5.1 The Three Models

  • One-factor: all 24 items load on a single general knowledge factor.
  • Two-factor: FL and EPL, freely correlated.
  • Three-factor: FL, EPL-Fin, and EPL-Legal, all freely correlated.

Each is nested in the next, so the added factors can be tested with scaled chi-square difference tests.

5.4 Robustness: Testing the 3-factor model against every 2-factor definition

The comparison above tests the three-factor model against a pre-defined two-factor model that separates FL items from EPL items. However, the three factors can be merged into two factors in three different ways, and a skeptic could reasonably ask whether these results depend on which 2-factor definition was chosen. This section was created to test the robustness of these results against alternative 2-factor definitions.

Table 18. Fit of All Five Single-Level Groupings
Model chi2 df CFI TLI RMSEA WRMR

A significant result means the simpler model fits significantly worse, i.e. the three-factor model is preferred.

Every 2-factor model, regardless of how the factors are grouped, fits significantly worse, and none of the comparisons is close to the .05 boundary. This shows that our results - that a 3-factor model fits substantially better than a 2-factor model - are not an artifact of how the 2-factor model happened to be defined. The 3-factor model also beats the two alternative 2-factor models.

If forced to pick a 2-factor model, 2F-B actually fits best. The 2-factor models all share the same degrees of freedom, so their chi-squares are directly comparable: 2F-B (\(\chi^2\) = 293.1) edges out 2F-A (\(\chi^2\) = 304.2), while 2F-C (\(\chi^2\) = 331.6) is far worse. So, the EPL-Fin factor actually aligns marginally better with FL than with EPL-Legal — but the gap is small, and the decisive fact is that 2F-C fails badly: EPL-Fin is not a free-floating block, it sits between the other two.

6 Question 2: Do each of the factors measure something meaningful on their own?

Question 1 established that the three factors are distinguishable. A model that distinguishes FL, EPL-Fin, and EPL-Legal fits the data better than models that collapse these domains together. However, the three factors are also strongly correlated (0.63–0.77), suggesting that much of what they measure is shared.

6.1 What this Question Asks

Suppose two FL items are correlated. That correlation could arise from at least two sources:

  1. A general source of knowledge or ability shared across the entire instrument. Someone who tends to perform well on FL items may also tend to perform well on EPL-Fin and EPL-Legal items.
  2. Something specific to FL. Even among people with the same level of general knowledge, some may be especially knowledgeable about the content covered by the FL items.

The correlated three-factor model does not separate these two sources. The FL factor represents everything the FL items have in common, including both the variance they share with the other domains and any variance that is unique to FL. The same is true for the EPL-Fin and EPL-Legal factors. Their strong correlations therefore tell us that the three domains share a substantial common component, but they do not tell us how much each domain measures beyond that common component.

The bifactor model separates these sources. It estimates a general factor that loads on all 24 items and, at the same time, a specific factor for each block. The specific FL factor therefore represents what the FL items still have in common after accounting for the general factor; likewise for EPL-Fin and EPL-Legal.

The key question is:

After accounting for the general factor shared across the instrument, do the items within each block still covary with one another in a systematic way?

If they do, the block contains reliable domain-specific information beyond the general factor. If little or no shared variance remains, then the factor is distinguishable in the overall covariance structure but contributes little evidence of a separate individual-difference dimension once the general factor is taken into account.

TipAn analogy: restaurant ratings

Imagine restaurants are evaluated using several questions about food, several about service, and several about atmosphere. Ratings across these domains will often correlate because restaurants that are good in one respect also tend to be good in others.

Question 1 asks whether food, service, and atmosphere are distinguishable dimensions. Do the food questions behave more similarly to one another than they do to the service or atmosphere questions? If so, treating the three domains separately describes the data better than treating every rating as a measure of one undifferentiated notion of restaurant quality.

Question 2 asks a different question. Once you account for a restaurant’s overall quality, ddo the food questions still move together in a way that is specifically about food? For example, among two restaurants with the same overall quality, can one be reliably better at food while the other is better at service?

If yes, a food sub-rating contains information beyond the overall rating. If no, the food questions mainly reflect overall restaurant quality, with little reliable food-specific information left over. In that case, differences between a restaurant’s overall score and its food subscore may largely reflect measurement noise rather than a stable, food-specific strength or weakness.

For one of our three factors, the answer turns out to be the second one.

One way to represent the commonality among the three factors is with a second-order model, in which a general literacy factor sits above FL, EPL-Fin, and EPL-Legal. The general factor accounts for what the three first-order factors share, while each first-order factor also retains residual variance of its own.

With only three first-order factors, however, this model has exactly the same fit as the correlated three-factor model (see Table 20 below). The second-order portion is just-identified: it can reproduce the three correlations among FL, EPL-Fin, and EPL-Legal exactly. Thus, although we can estimate higher-order loadings, the data cannot tell us whether this higher-order representation provides a better explanation of the correlations than simply allowing the three factors to correlate.

To ask the more specific question above—whether each domain retains coherent variance after accounting for what all of the items share—we instead fit a bifactor model. In this model, the general factor and the three domain-specific factors are estimated simultaneously at the item level. Each item loads directly on the general factor as well as on its own specific factor, allowing us to separate variance shared across the entire instrument from variance unique to each domain.

Table 20. Second-Order vs. Correlated Three-Factor
Model chi2 df CFI TLI RMSEA WRMR
Correlated three-factor 283.9 249 0.971 0.968 0.023 0.887
Second-order 283.9 249 0.971 0.968 0.023 0.887
Identical fit and degrees of freedom: the second-order level is just-identified with three first-order factors, so this is a reparameterisation rather than a rival model.

6.2 Testing the Bifactor Model

Caution

I am still working through some of the technical details in this section and the following sections, so the interpretation below should be treated as provisional for now.

In a bifactor model, the general factor loads on every item directly, and each specific factor is fitted to its own items at the same time. The general and specific factors are forced to be uncorrelated, so they cannot claim the same variance twice. Each item’s variance therefore splits cleanly into three parts: what it shares with all 24 items, what it shares only with its own block, and noise.

NoteInterpreting the diagram

The general factor is the part every item has in common. The specific factors are what is left inside each block after that part has been taken out — the food-specific signal in the restaurant analogy above. Because the two are forced to be uncorrelated, a specific factor can only exist if its block’s items still hang together once the general factor has taken its share.

6.3 Fitting the Model

Estimating the full bifactor — general factor plus all three specific factors — produces a degenerate solution rather than an answer.

Table 21. The EPL-Fin Specific Factor Collapses
Parameter Estimate
EPL-Fin specific =~ ep_10 0.001
EPL-Fin specific =~ ep_11 0.002
EPL-Fin specific =~ ep_12 104.155
Residual variance of ep_12 -10848
lavaan also reports that the information matrix cannot be inverted, so this model has no standard errors and no robust fit statistics.

Two of the three EPL-Fin specific loadings sit at zero, the third runs away, and ep_12 absorbs an impossible negative residual variance. This is the answer to Question 2 for that block, not a failure to obtain one. A specific factor can only be estimated if there is leftover covariance to estimate it from, and here there is none: once the general factor has taken its share, the three financial-consequence items no longer hang together at all. They correlate with each other only to the extent that they correlate with everything else on the instrument.

In the restaurant analogy, this is the case where the food ratings carry no food-specific signal — they are just the overall impression, recorded a third time.

Two ways of making the model estimable both confirm it:

Table 22. Bifactor Variants
Model chi2 df CFI TLI RMSEA WRMR
Correlated three-factor (Question 1) 283.9 249 0.971 0.968 0.023 0.887
Bifactor, all three specific factors -- 228 -- -- -- 0.828
Bifactor, EPL-Fin loadings constrained equal 263.5 230 0.972 0.967 0.023 0.833
Bifactor, EPL-Fin specific factor removed 265.4 231 0.971 0.966 0.024 0.837
Constraining the three EPL-Fin specific loadings to a common value turns the question into a single-parameter test: that loading is 0.307 (SE 0.098, p = 0.002, 95% CI [0.114, 0.499]). Deleting the factor entirely costs almost nothing in fit. Bifactor models are not nested in the correlated three-factor model, so fit is compared descriptively.

The remaining analysis uses the reduced bifactor — general factor, FL specific factor, EPL-Legal specific factor, with the EPL-Fin items loading on the general factor only. It estimates cleanly with all residual variances positive.

6.4 How Much Is General, How Much Is Specific?

Table 23. How the Variance Divides
Index Value
ECV — share of common variance held by the general factor 0.726
omega-H — share of total-score variance held by the general factor 0.829
omega — total reliability of the full scale 0.921
omega-H / omega — share of *reliable* variance that is general 0.901
omega-HS, FL specific factor 0.080

Items whose common variance is mostly specific (I-ECV < .50) 6 of 24
omega-HS is the share of a subscale score's variance attributable to its own specific factor once the general factor is removed. Values below about .50 mean a subscale score is mostly not measuring anything of its own.

The answer to Question 2, block by block:

  • FL: ωHS = 0.08. An FL subscore is roughly 8% “financial literacy specifically” and the rest general knowledge.
  • EPL-Legal: ωHS = 0.41. This is the block with the most distinctive content, and even it does not clear the ~.50 usually required to interpret a subscore on its own.
  • EPL-Fin: none. The specific factor cannot be estimated because there is no leftover covariance to estimate it from. These three items are, measurement-wise, three more indicators of general knowledge that happen to be phrased in estate language.

Overall, 73% of the common variance across the 24 items belongs to the general factor, and 90% of the reliable variance in a total score is general-factor variance.

It is not pure unidimensionality, though. 6 of 24 items have more of their common variance in the specific factor than in the general one — ep_7 (retirement account beneficiary vs. will) most of all, at 82% specific. Real domain structure exists. It is outweighed, not absent.

WarningTwo caveats on the bifactor

It flatters itself. Bifactor models fit better than their competitors close to mechanically, because extra orthogonal factors absorb residual covariance whether or not a general factor is substantively real. Its good fit is not evidence for a general factor; the variance shares are the informative output, not the fit indices.

The reduced model is data-driven. Deleting the EPL-Fin specific factor after seeing the full model fail is a decision made in light of the data. It is well justified here — two independent repairs agree, and the constrained loading is only 0.31 (95% CI [0.11, 0.50]), and freeing the three loadings makes the factor collapse altogether — but the indices above inherit that choice, so treat them as approximate. Bifactor indices from binary items under WLSMV are also less well studied than their continuous-data counterparts.

7 Reconciling the Two Answers

The two questions give answers that sound contradictory:

  • Question 1: the three-factor model fits significantly better than one factor. The blocks are distinguishable.
  • Question 2: 73% of the common variance belongs to a single general factor, and one block has no specific variance at all.

These results are not contradictory. They speak to different questions.

7.1 What Each Test Actually Asks

Table 24. The Two Questions Side by Side
Question 1 (model comparison) Question 2 (variance partition)
The question Are these factors the same thing? How much variance do these factors share?
The quantity Is the correlation between factors reliably below 1.0? What proportion of common variance is general vs. specific?
The answer here No, they are not the same thing (p < .001) Most of it is shared (ECV = 0.73)
What it licenses Modelling them separately; treating EPL as its own construct Reporting a total score; treating the scale as essentially one dimension for scoring
What it does NOT license Claiming they are independent, or that subscores are meaningful Claiming the blocks are interchangeable, or that a one-factor model is correct

The crucial point is that a difference can be statistically reliable and substantively small at the same time. The chi-square difference test asks whether the correlation between two factors is distinguishable from a perfect 1.0. It does not ask whether the correlation is low. With N = 268, a correlation of 0.82 is comfortably distinguishable from 1.0 — and 0.82 still means the two factors share 67% of their variance.

Your own fit indices show the same thing from the other direction. The one-factor model — the model that says all 24 items measure one thing — already achieves CFI = 0.931. That is not a disaster; it is a mediocre-but-recognisable fit. The three-factor model improves it to 0.971. The improvement is real and statistically significant, and it is also an improvement on a model that was already capturing most of the structure. “Significantly better than one factor” and “one factor gets you most of the way” are both true statements about the same numbers.

7.2 Analogies to Aid Interpretation of Results

TipThree analogies

The decathlon. Sprinting, hurdling, and the long jump are genuinely different events. A coach can tell them apart, athletes specialise, and nobody would claim they are the same skill — that is Question 1. But most of what determines how well someone does across all three is general athleticism: strength, speed, coordination. That is Question 2. Both are true. The practical consequence is exactly what we recommend here: to rank decathletes overall, use the total score; to decide who should run the hurdles specifically, you would need the event-specific part — and in our data that part is measured too unreliably to use.

Siblings. Three siblings are unmistakably different people; you would never confuse them, and a statistical test would separate them instantly. Yet most of what makes each of them look the way they do is shared family resemblance. “Reliably distinguishable” and “mostly the same underlying thing” are not in tension — they are the normal state of affairs for things that come from a common source.

Zoom level on a map. Zoomed in, you see three distinct neighbourhoods with their own boundaries and character. Zoomed out, it is obviously one city. Neither view is wrong; they answer different questions. Question 1 is the zoomed-in view, Question 2 the zoomed-out one, and a good write-up reports both.

7.3 Where Individual Participants Sit

The variance decompositions above are statements about the sample as a whole. It is worth seeing what the overlap looks like person by person: if FL and EPL were effectively the same thing, participants would fall along a single diagonal and nobody would be strong on one and weak on the other.

The cloud is elongated along the diagonal — that is the shared general factor, and it is the dominant feature. But the off-diagonal corners are not empty. Splitting each scale at its median puts 45 participants above the EPL median while below the FL median, and 35 the other way round: 80 of 268 (30%) are discordant on a simple median split.

The same point without relying on a median split: 31 participants score at least a full standard deviation higher on EPL than on FL, and 49 score at least a standard deviation higher on FL than on EPL — 80 people, or 30% of the sample, for whom the two scores would tell a materially different story.

This is the person-level counterpart to everything above. A correlation of 0.52 between the observed totals leaves real room for individual mismatch, which is why the scales are worth administering separately even though a single total score is the right way to report them.

7.4 What This Means in Practice

  • Keep the three-factor model as the measurement model. It fits best, and a one-factor model is statistically rejected. If you are estimating relationships between EPL and other variables, model it as its own factor.
  • Report a total score, not subscores. The general factor carries 90% of the reliable variance; the FL and EPL-Legal subscores carry 0.08 and 0.41 of their own. An EPL-Fin subscore should not be reported at all.
  • Do not describe the constructs as independent. They share 40–67% of their variance. “Distinguishable” is the correct word; “distinct” or “separate” oversells it.
  • Let the validity evidence carry the argument. The strongest case that EPL is worth measuring is not the factor structure — it is Section 8, where estate planning engagement is associated with EPL net of financial literacy while the reverse partial correlation is zero. High overlap in variance is compatible with the non-overlapping part being the part that matters.

8 Is Estate Planning Engagement Related to EPL Above and Beyond FL?

This section relates the scales to a behavioral measure available in the data, the number of estate planning actions a participant has already completed (will, trust, beneficiary designations, power of attorney; 0–4). We refer to this variable below as EP engagement.

The question addressed is:

Is EP engagement related to estate planning literacy over and above what it shares with financial literacy?

8.1 Zero-Order Associations

First, we examine the correlations between all three factors - split and then, EPL combined - and EP engagement.

All factors are related to EP engagement, and estate planning literacy more so than financial literacy: r = 0.252 versus 0.164 for financial literacy. Because the FL and EPL factors are themselves correlated at 0.52, the difference between those two correlations should be tested using a method that accounts for dependent correlations.

Table 26. Is EPL More Strongly Related to Engagement than FL Is?
Comparison r (EPL) r (FL) Difference t p
EPL vs. FL, correlation with EP engagement 0.252 0.164 +0.088 1.5 0.134
Steiger's test for two dependent correlations sharing one variable (EP engagement).

The difference in correlation strength is 0.088 (p = 0.134), which does not reach conventional significance in this age-restricted sample. EPL is numerically the more strongly associated of the two, but with n = 268 the zero-order difference on its own is not decisive; the partial correlations in Section 8.2 are the sharper test and they do separate the two scales.

8.2 Above and Beyond: Partial Correlations

The zero-order correlations do not answer the question on their own, because FL and EPL overlap heavily. A partial correlation removes that overlap: the correlation between EP engagement and EPL, with financial literacy held constant, is the association that survives after everything the two scales share has been taken out of both.

Table 27. Association with EP Engagement, Net of the Other Scale
Association Held constant Partial r Partial p Semipartial r Unique share of engagement variance
EP engagement - EPL Financial literacy 0.198 0.001 0.195 3.8%
EP engagement - FL Estate planning literacy 0.040 0.513 0.039 0.2%
Partial r removes the other scale from both variables and is symmetric — it makes no claim about which variable is the cause. Semipartial r removes the other scale from the literacy measure only; its square is the share of engagement variance uniquely associated with that scale.
ImportantEPL may be worth measuring separately

Holding financial literacy constant, EP engagement remains associated with estate planning literacy at r = 0.198 (p = 0.001).

Holding estate planning literacy constant, the association with financial literacy is only r = 0.040 (p = 0.513), which is not significantly different from zero.

In other words, the entire association between financial literacy and estate planning engagement is accounted for by what financial literacy shares with EPL. Once that shared part is removed, nothing is left. The reverse is not true: EPL retains a clear association after FL is removed, uniquely accounting for 3.8% of the variance in engagement against 0.2% for FL.

This matters because Sections 5 and 6 found the two factors share most of their variance — which on its own looks like a discriminant validity problem. The part they do not share turns out to be the part that may be related to behavior.

The claim here is comparative, not a claim about magnitude. In absolute terms 3.8% is a small share of variance, and Section 8.3 takes that seriously rather than glossing it.

Table 28. The Two EPL Subscales, Net of Financial Literacy
Association Held constant Partial r Partial p Semipartial r
EP engagement - EPL-Legal Financial literacy 0.195 0.001 0.192
EP engagement - EPL-Fin Financial literacy 0.090 0.141 0.089

Both EPL subscales retain an association with engagement after financial literacy is removed, the legal/administrative block more strongly.

8.3 How Big Is This, Really?

Uniquely accounting for 3.8% of the variance in engagement is, in absolute terms, small. It is worth being direct about that rather than letting a percentage do rhetorical work.

Table 29. Putting the Variance Shares in Context
Quantity Value
Variance in engagement explained by age alone 3.4%
Variance explained by FL and EPL together 6.5%
Variance explained by age, FL, and EPL together 8.4%
Unique share attributable to EPL 3.8%
Unique share attributable to FL 0.2%

Age alone explains more of who has done estate planning than both knowledge scales combined. In other words, whether a person has a will is mostly a function of how old they are. Knowledge appears to be one modest input among many.

Two things nonetheless keep the result meaningful.

1. The same association looks larger expressed as a group difference. Squaring a correlation makes it look small; it is the same number either way.

Table 30. EPL Score by Whether Any Estate Planning Has Been Done

Participants who have done nothing score 5.60 on the 12-item EPL scale; those who have done anything at all score 7.26. That is 0.62 standard deviations — a medium-to-large difference by conventional benchmarks — and it is the same fact as the modest r. “Explains 3.8% of variance” and “a gap of roughly two-thirds of a standard deviation” describe one relationship.

Knowledge and action come apart for a substantial minority. The group means above compress a joint distribution that is worth seeing in full, because the mismatched cells are the ones that matter for whether EPL is worth measuring at all.

Reading down the rows, the association is visible but loose: the share who have completed nothing falls as EPL rises, yet it never approaches zero. Of the 82 participants in the top quarter of the EPL distribution (scores of 9 or higher), 11 have completed no estate planning at all and 41 have completed at most one step, against 32% completing nothing among everyone below that cut. Only 8 of them have completed all four.

That group is the practically interesting one. They are not failing to plan because they do not understand what a will or a beneficiary designation does; whatever is stopping them sits somewhere other than knowledge. It is also a direct illustration of why the association in this section is real but modest, and why Section 9.2 finds that knowledge does not predict what the unengaged expect to do next.

2. Small effects are the norm in this literature, and FL’s result here is ordinary. The financial literacy items come from Fernandes, Lynch and Netemeyer’s (2014) meta-analysis, which reports two findings that are often run together but are quite different. Interventions to improve financial literacy accounted for roughly 0.1% of the variance in the downstream financial behaviours studied. Measured financial literacy did considerably better — on the order of 1–2% of variance — though those effects attenuated substantially once psychological covariates omitted from earlier work were included.

Our FL result belongs to the second category and sits right in that range. Its zero-order association with EP engagement is r = 0.164, or 2.7% of the variance — slightly above the meta-analytic benchmark for measured literacy, and unremarkable for this literature. Financial literacy is behaving here about as it usually does.

What is notable is not the size of FL’s association but where it goes. Almost all of that 2.7% is variance it shares with estate planning literacy. FL’s unique contribution is 0.2%, against 3.8% for EPL. So financial literacy is related to estate planning behaviour — but through what it holds in common with estate planning knowledge, not through financial knowledge as such.

NoteSection Summary

The value of this section is discriminant: it shows the EPL items capture something behaviorally relevant that the FL items do not. It is not an effect-size claim, and it should not be written up as one.

NoteWhat this does and does not establish

It establishes that EP engagement is related to estate planning literacy in a way that financial literacy cannot account for, and that the reverse does not hold.

It does not establish direction. Someone who has drafted a will may score higher on EPL because they went through the process — a professional explained beneficiary designations to them — rather than having acted because they already knew. Both readings are consistent with these numbers, as is a third in which family circumstances drive both. Describe the finding as an association net of financial literacy, not as evidence that knowledge causes action.

9 Exploratory Analyses

In the survey, we included several additional measures that were not part of the measurement question. The measures are analyzed below for exploratory purposes.

9.1 How Participants Used the Intention and Expectation Scales

Participants rated seven behaviours twice: how much they intend to do each one (bi_*) and how likely they think they actually are to do it (be_*), both on 1–9 scales. Because the “update” wording only appeared for actions a participant had already completed, the draft/update variants are combined into a single item per behaviour.

The shape of these distributions governs how every correlation involving them should be read, so it is worth establishing first.

Table 33. Composite Intentions and Expectations
Measure Mean SD 25th Median 75th % all seven = 1 % mean >= 7 Skew
Intentions (BI) 3.85 2.48 1.43 3.29 6.04 19.4 16.8 +0.39

These are not low-but-otherwise-ordinary distributions — they are bimodal. There is a wall at the bottom of the scale, a near-empty middle, and a smaller second cluster at the top. Only 3.5% of expectation responses and 2.9% of intention responses use the scale midpoint of 4. Participants are largely sorting themselves into “definitely not” and “probably yes” rather than expressing degrees of likelihood.

ImportantTwo different floor statistics

These are easy to confuse and they answer different questions.

44.7% of individual expectation responses are 1. This pools every participant and every item, so someone who answers 1 for “consult a lawyer” and 6 for “seek information” contributes to it once.

25.7% of participants answered 1 to all seven items. This counts people who are at the floor on everything.

The corresponding intention figures are 36.8% and 19.4%. Both statistics are reported below; the figure above shows the response-level version, and the composite table shows the person-level one.

Intentions run consistently above expectations. The paired difference is +0.74 points (p < .001), with the two correlated at r = 0.764. Participants report intending to do more than they think they will actually do — which is the distinction the two measures are meant to capture, so the gap is a point in the measures’ favour.

The ordering across behaviours is sensible. Seeking information sits highest and consulting a lawyer lowest, with the share of floor responses tracking the cost and effort of each behaviour almost perfectly.

NoteWhat this shape means for the correlations that follow

Variance is not restricted — the composite SD is 2.20 on a nine-point scale and the full range is used. The complication is the shape, in two ways.

Censoring at the floor. Everyone whose true position sits at or below the bottom of the scale is stacked on 1, which compresses real differences among the least-likely participants and attenuates correlations.

A sparse middle. With few observations between 4 and 6, the linear relationship Pearson correlations assume is a poor description of the data. This is why rank-order (Spearman) estimates run somewhat higher than Pearson estimates throughout this section.

The practical consequence is that correlations with these measures largely distinguish who is at the floor from who is not, rather than tracking fine gradations of enthusiasm. They should be read that way.

9.2 Expectations Among Those Who Have Not Yet Acted

Section 8 showed that EPL tracks what people have already done. That association is open to a reverse reading: going through the process may teach people the material, rather than knowing the material prompting the action.

The participants who report completing none of the four actions offer a partial way in. They have no estate planning experience to have learned from, so any association between their knowledge and their expectations of acting cannot be explained by their having already acted. If knowing more moves people toward acting, the better-informed members of this group should be the ones closest to acting.

One feature of the survey design helps here. Participants only saw the “update” wording for actions they had already taken, so everyone in this subgroup saw the same seven initiate items and answered all of them. There is no differential missingness within the group to complicate the comparison.

Expectations were rated on a 1–9 scale. The seven items cohere strongly in this subgroup (alpha = 0.95), so they are also averaged into a single composite.

Table 35. Composite Expectations, Knowledge and Age (No Prior Actions)
Association r 95% CI p
Expectations - EPL score -0.031 [-0.266, 0.207] 0.797
Expectations - FL score -0.098 [-0.327, 0.142] 0.425
Expectations - age 0.106 [-0.134, 0.334] 0.387
EPL score - age 0.207 [-0.031, 0.423] 0.088

n = 69. The last two rows are included for contrast: age is related to knowledge in this subgroup even though it is not related to expectations.

Neither knowledge nor age is related to what these participants expect to do. The composite association with EPL is r = -0.031 (p = 0.797) and with age r = 0.106 (p = 0.387). No individual behaviour reaches significance for either predictor, and the strongest of the fourteen item-level tests is p = 0.170. Rank-order correlations are somewhat larger — Spearman’s rho is 0.028 for EPL and 0.100 for age — which is what one would expect given the floor in the outcome, but neither reaches conventional significance either.

Age is not simply inert in this group. Within the same 69 participants, age still tracks the literacy scales: r = 0.207 with EPL (p = 0.088) and r = 0.349 with FL (p = 0.003) – both positive, though only the FL association clears p < .05 in this smaller, age-truncated subgroup. Older participants who have not acted still tend to know more. They are no closer to acting.

NoteHow much weight this null can carry

Three limits are worth stating plainly.

Power. With 69 participants, the smallest correlation detectable at 80% power is about 0.33. This analysis can rule out a moderate association; it cannot rule out a small one.

Floor effects. Expectations are low and bunched — the subgroup mean is 2.80 on the 1–9 scale, and 36% answered 1 to all seven items. As set out in Section 9.1, the issue is not restricted variance but censoring at the floor together with a sparse middle, which attenuates correlations and is part of why the rank-order estimates run higher than the Pearson ones.

Selection. People who have completed nothing are not a random subset. Whatever keeps them from acting may also compress their expectations, and that common cause is not measured here.

Taken together with Section 8, the pattern is that estate planning literacy tracks what people have done but not what they expect to do. That is easier to reconcile with a doing-teaches-knowing account than with a knowing-prompts-doing one, though neither is established by these data. It is also consistent with the wider finding, familiar from the intention–behaviour literature, that stated expectations are weak proxies for the behaviour itself.

One further contrast points the same way. Among the 198 participants who have completed at least one action, expectations run higher (3.24 versus 2.80, p = 0.147) and relate to age in the opposite direction (r = -0.085, p = 0.236) — older participants who have already acted expect to do less, which is what one would expect if they have less left to do. Both reach p < .05 in the all-ages document; here neither does, which is what the narrower age range and smaller n would predict rather than a change in the underlying pattern.

9.3 Prior Exposure to the Financial Literacy Items

After answering the knowledge items, participants rated how certain they were that they had seen each FL item prior to taking our survey. The item exp_8 is excluded to match the exclusion of fin_8, leaving 12 ratings that pair one-to-one with the 12 FL items.

If participants have seen these items before, then part of what FL measures is prior exposure rather than knowledge.

Participants who report having seen these items before do score higher on financial literacy (r = 0.187, p = 0.002), and the effect is visible item by item (see Table 32 above).

The exposure measure also behaves sensibly relative to the EPL items: prior exposure to the FL items correlates about 2.7 times as strongly with FL as with EPL (r = 0.070). This is what we would expect if prior exposure to the items improves one’s performance on them.

Thus, some of the FL score reflects item familiarity rather than financial knowledge, which is a known hazard of reusing a widely circulated battery on an online panel. It is a modest effect and it does not threaten the measurement conclusions — but it is a reason to prefer the EPL items when a clean knowledge measure is wanted, and a reason to consider refreshing the FL battery in future waves.

9.3.1 Does Prior Exposure Affect the Factor Structure?

If familiarity is inflating FL scores but not EPL scores, this could explain why the three-factor model fit the data best. Here, for robustness, I refit the models on participants who report little or no prior exposure to the FL items.

Exposure is widespread — the median rating is 2.92 on the 1–5 scale — so there is no clean “never seen these” group to fall back on. The models are therefore refit at three progressively stricter cut-offs rather than just using one arbitrary cutoff.

Table 38. Factor Models Refit Excluding Participants Who Report Prior Exposure
Sample N 1F CFI 2F CFI 3F CFI Best fit H1 p H2 p
All participants 268 0.931 0.956 0.971 Three-factor < .001 < .001
Exposure <= 3.5 185 0.951 0.960 0.975 Three-factor 0.015 0.005
Exposure <= 3.0 144 0.953 0.959 0.979 Three-factor 0.032 0.005
Exposure <= 2.5 105 0.970 0.971 0.979 Three-factor 0.253 0.100
Exposure is the mean of the 12 prior-exposure ratings (1 = certain never seen, 5 = certain seen before). H1 compares the two-factor model against one factor; H2 compares three factors against two.

The three-factor model fits best in every subsample, and both comparisons stay significant at p < .01 throughout. Excluding the most exposure-prone participants does not undermine the structure.

Two things to note when reading this. The chi-square difference values shrink as the samples get smaller due to lower statistical power. The one-factor model actually fits slightly better in the restricted samples, so the gap between one and three factors narrows a little.

To avoid losing statistical power by removing participants, in the section below, I keep everyone in the sample and model prior exposure as a predictor of the latent factors.

9.3.2 Modelling Exposure Directly (MIMIC)

Excluding participants throws away data and only answers whether the 3-factor structure survives. A MIMIC model (multiple indicators, multiple causes) keeps everyone and puts exposure into the model as a predictor of the latent factors. That allows us to answer the question: how much of each factor is prior familiarity rather than knowledge?

Table 39. Effect of Prior Exposure on Each Latent Factor
Factor Standardized effect of exposure SE 95% CI p Variance explained

Exposure is the mean of the 12 prior-exposure ratings, entered as a continuous predictor of each latent factor. Items remain ordered and the model is estimated with WLSMV.

Exposure predicts financial literacy. The standardized effect on FL is 0.195 (p = 0.006), against 0.136 for EPL-financial (p = 0.134) and 0.041 for EPL-legal (p = 0.576). Only the FL path is clearly non-zero — which is what should happen if the measure is picking up genuine recognition of a recycled item battery rather than a general tendency to claim familiarity.

Only about 4% of the financial literacy factor is attributable to prior exposure; the remaining 96% is not. This doesn’t seem like that much contamination. For the two EPL factors the figures are 1.8% and 0.2% — negligible.

9.4 Superstition

A single item asked how strongly participants agreed with the statement: “I am a superstitious person.”

Table 41. Superstition, Engagement, and Literacy
Association r 95% CI p
Superstition - prior EP engagement 0.004 [-0.116, 0.125] 0.944
Superstition - EPL score 0.016 [-0.105, 0.136] 0.799

Excludes 2 participant(s) coded 6, taken to be "prefer not to answer" given its frequency; confirm against the instrument. n = 266.

Superstition is unrelated to estate planning engagement. The correlation is 0.004 — essentially exactly zero — and the group means are flat across all five levels. If the hypothesis was that superstitious people avoid estate planning because it means contemplating death, these data give it no support at all.

It may be related to estate planning literacy, though in a non-linear way (it appears more inverted-U shaped). It also negatively relates to financial literacy; the association is negative and clearly non-zero (r = -0.170, p = 0.005).

9.5 Death Attitudes

The DAP-R (Wong, Reker & Gesser, 1994) is a 32-item, five-dimension measure of attitudes toward death, rated 1–7. The published structure includes the following facotrs: Fear of Death, Death Avoidance, Neutral Acceptance, Approach Acceptance, and Escape Acceptance. In this sample, the items from the scale generally reproduce the original structure. Expand the section below for additional details.

The correlations reproduce the pattern reported in the original validation: Fear of Death and Death Avoidance are strongly related (r = 0.71) — both are negative orientations toward death — and Approach and Escape Acceptance go together (r = 0.52), since both frame death as desirable. Neutral Acceptance stands largely apart from the rest, as it should: regarding death as an ordinary fact is not the same as welcoming or dreading it.

Verdict: the published structure replicates.

Parallel analysis recovers exactly five factors, 94% of items load on their intended subscale, the five-factor CFA fits acceptably while a one-factor model does not, and the factor intercorrelations reproduce the expected pattern.

The one qualification is Neutral Acceptance, which is the weakest subscale on every diagnostic: the lowest alpha, both of the misplaced items, and both of the sub-.40 loadings. Dropping dapr_31 and dapr_32 raises CFI to 0.944. This is a known soft spot in the DAP-R rather than a problem with this sample.

The various DAP-R factors correlate to prior EP engagement, behavioral intentions, and behavioral expectations in different ways.

Table 47. Death Attitudes, Superstition, and the Three Behavioural Measures
Measure Mean (SD) EP engagement Intentions Expectations
Fear of death 3.52 (1.54) -0.104 +0.133* +0.205**
Death avoidance 3.63 (1.63) -0.081 +0.125* +0.143*
Neutral acceptance 5.38 (0.92) +0.190** -0.029 -0.090

* p < .05, ** p < .01. DAP-R subscales are means of 1-7 ratings; superstition is a single 1-5 item excluding the 6 participants coded 6. EP engagement is the count of estate planning actions already completed.

Some patterns worth noting.

Attitudes line up sensibly with what people have actually done. Fear of death (-0.104) and death avoidance (-0.081) go with less completed estate planning; approach acceptance (+0.115) and neutral acceptance (+0.190) go with more. Being able to contemplate death calmly is associated with having done the paperwork; avoiding the thought is associated with not having.

But these attitudes do not line up with what people say they will do in the near future. Nearly every measure correlates positively with intentions and expectations — including fear of death and and death avoidance.

Adjusting for that shared dimension separates the two cleanly. Holding it constant, the engagement associations survive and sharpen — death avoidance -0.121, approach acceptance +0.108 — while every intention and expectation association falls to nothing. So the content of a person’s death attitude relates to their behaviour; only the intensity relates to their stated plans.

Superstition is unrelated to prior estate planning engagement. Its correlation with completed actions is +0.004 — flat across all five levels (Figure 14). It relates only to expectations (+0.195) and, as shown earlier, to financial literacy.

NoteHow to read this

Two cautions. First, all of these correlations are small — the largest is about 0.20, so death attitudes may only be a minor part of the picture.

This is exploratory. The measures were collected for descriptive purposes, nothing here was planned in advance, and none of it should be reported as a test of a hypothesis.

9.6 Reading Correlations With Expectations

Every association with expectations reported above is around r = .20. Because Section 9.1 showed the outcome is censored at the floor, it is worth asking whether that ceiling on the correlations is an artefact of the scale or a real description of the effects.

Unreliability in the outcome is not the constraint. The expectations composite has alpha = 0.937, which caps an observed correlation at 96.8% of its true value — a cost of roughly 3%. Note that superstitious is a single item, however, so its own unreliability is unknown and is likely to attenuate its correlation by more than this.

Table 48. Censoring at the Floor: Tobit Versus OLS Slopes
Predictor OLS b Tobit b Ratio
Has children 0.343 0.490 1.43
Superstition 0.454 0.652 1.44
Approach acceptance 0.310 0.346 1.12
Fear of death 0.451 0.563 1.25
Death avoidance 0.314 0.396 1.26
Predictors standardised, so slopes are points on the 1-9 expectation scale per SD. Tobit models treat the 69 participants (25.7%) at the floor as left-censored. A ratio above 1 means OLS understates the underlying slope.

Censoring does attenuate these estimates, by 12% to 44% depending on the predictor. The observed correlations understate the underlying relationships — but not by enough to change the verdict. Fully disattenuated, these associations would sit near r = .25 to .30, which is an ordinary individual-differences effect. There is no large effect concealed beneath the floor.

It is worth separating two questions that the p-values blur together. At n = 268, a correlation of .20 returns p < .001. That is a fact about the sample size, not about the size of the effect; the correlation still describes about 4% of the variance either way.

Table 49. Two Ways a Predictor Can Relate to Expectations
Predictor r (all) r (above floor) OR for being at floor p (floor)
Has children +0.156 +0.108 0.73 0.019
Superstition +0.206 +0.119 0.57 < .001
Approach acceptance +0.141 +0.198 0.97 0.855
Fear of death +0.205 +0.200 0.78 0.080
Death avoidance +0.143 +0.138 0.83 0.205
The odds ratio is per SD, from a logistic regression predicting whether a participant answered 1 to all seven items. An odds ratio below 1 means higher scorers are less likely to be at the floor. The middle column recomputes the correlation among participants above the floor only.

The predictors divide into two kinds, which the correlation alone conceals.

Children and superstition operate at the floor. Both predict whether a participant is disengaged altogether (odds ratios of 0.73 and 0.57 per SD), and both correlations collapse once floor cases are removed. What they explain is who is completely disengaged, not how eager the rest are.

Approach acceptance and fear of death operate above the floor. Neither predicts floor membership, and their correlations survive or strengthen when floor cases are dropped. They track gradations among participants already contemplating action.

The two kinds produce nearly identical correlations while describing quite different relationships, which is a reason to prefer the decomposition over the single coefficient.

Table 50. The Same Findings Expressed as Rates of Complete Disengagement
Predictor Group Higher group Lower group Difference
Has children Has children vs not 21.3% 34.9% -13.5 pts
Superstition Above vs below median 14.2% 33.3% -19.2 pts
Approach acceptance Above vs below median 24.4% 27.0% -2.6 pts
Cells give the percentage of each group answering 1 to all seven expectation items.

Expressed this way, participants without children are 1.6 times as likely to be completely disengaged as parents, and low-superstition participants 2.4 times as likely as high-superstition ones. This is the same information as “r = .20”, and it is a more faithful description of what the data contain.

NoteRecommendation for the next wave

The floor is doing enough work here that it is worth designing around. Two options: extend the response scale downward so that “definitely will not” is distinguishable from “have not thought about it”, or ask a screening question first and route only engaged participants to the likelihood ratings. Either would recover the variance that censoring is currently discarding.

10 Robustness Across Age Cut-offs

Everything above is computed on the 35+ sample. Because that cut-off is a judgement call rather than a property of the data, this section refits the central analyses at three nested cut-offs — all ages, 25+, and 35+ — so the reader can see which conclusions depend on it and which do not.

The three samples are nested, so they are not independent replications: a quantity that moves smoothly across the columns is partly doing so by construction. Read the table for whether a conclusion survives, not as three separate estimates.

10.1 What Survives and What Does Not

The measurement conclusions are stable. Both model comparisons stay significant at every cut-off, the three-factor model keeps the best fit, the EPL-Fin specific factor stays unidentified, and total-scale reliability barely moves. Nothing in Sections 5 or 6 depends on which age cut-off is used.

The partial-correlation result is stable. EPL retains its association with engagement net of FL at every cut-off, and FL’s partial correlation net of EPL stays indistinguishable from zero at every cut-off. This is the load-bearing finding of Section 8, and the age cut-off does not touch it.

Two things are cut-off dependent, and they should be reported as such.

The Steiger test. The zero-order EPL-versus-FL difference is significant in the full sample and not significant at either restricted cut-off. It fails already at 25+, so this is not a fact about older participants — it is the most marginal test in the document, sitting just under the conventional threshold in the full sample and falling out as soon as any subgroup is removed. The comparative claim should rest on the partial correlations, which are stable, rather than on this test.

The FL specific factor. Omega-HS for FL is broadly unchanged from all ages to 25+ and then collapses at 35+. The entire movement is produced by the participants in the 25-34 band, and resampling indicates this index is unstable at these sample sizes: random subsamples of the all-ages data at n = 268 produce values below .15 more than one time in ten. The 35+ value should not be read as evidence that financial literacy has no specific factor among older adults. Testing that properly would require a multi-group model with age as the grouping variable and invariance constraints on the specific loadings, which this sample is too small to support.

One trend runs consistently in the same direction. EPL-Fin degrades as the cut-off rises: its alpha falls across the three columns while its correlation with financial literacy rises. That is the same direction at both cut-offs and reinforces the recommendation in Section 11.1 to rebuild the block — among the older participants the instrument is aimed at, the three financial-consequence items are at their least distinguishable from plain financial literacy.

11 Conclusions

Table 52. Summary of Findings
Question Answer Evidence
Q1: Is EPL distinguishable from FL? Yes Two-factor beats one-factor, chi2(1) = 19.2, p < .001.
Q1: Are EPL's two dimensions distinguishable? Yes Three-factor beats two-factor, chi2(2) = 14.4, p < .001; also beats both alternative merges.
Q2: How much variance is general rather than block-specific? Most of it Bifactor ECV = 0.73; omega-HS = 0.08 (FL) and 0.41 (EPL-Legal); EPL-Fin specific factor not estimable.
Is EP engagement related to EPL net of FL? Yes r = 0.25 zero-order; partial r = 0.20 holding FL constant (p 0.001).
Is EP engagement related to FL net of EPL? No Partial r = 0.04 holding EPL constant (p = 0.51) - indistinguishable from zero.
Should FL / EPL subscores be reported? Total scale yes, subscores no omega-H / omega = 0.90 of reliable total-score variance is general; subscale alphas 0.74 / 0.63 / 0.53.

What to claim. Estate planning literacy is empirically distinguishable from financial literacy, its two dimensions are distinguishable from each other, and — the part that matters — estate planning engagement is associated with EPL over and above financial literacy, while the reverse association is indistinguishable from zero.

What not to claim. That these are independent abilities. They share most of their variance, and the EPL-Fin block has no identifiable unique variance at all.

11.1 Are the Items Good Enough?

Overall, the items are psychometrically sound but the EPL-Fin subscale is not.

The items themselves behave well. All 24 loadings fall between 0.34 and 0.80, no item is at floor or ceiling, and total-scale alpha is 0.81. This is not a set of broken items.

The overlap between factors is probably real, not an artifact. One plausible artifact was scoring “I don’t know” as incorrect: someone who skips a lot scores low on everything, which could manufacture a general factor. It does not. Refitting the two-factor model with blanks treated as genuinely missing rather than wrong raises the FL–EPL latent correlation from 0.76 to 0.88. Restricting attention to items people actually attempted makes the constructs look more alike, not less.

The potential weak point is EPL-Fin. The three items have a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.53, a correlation of 0.82 with financial literacy, a second-order loading of 0.96, and — the decisive finding — no estimable specific factor once the general factor is removed.

Suggestions for the next wave (this is what Claude - not necessarily I - recommends).

  • Rebuild EPL-Fin around knowledge, not arithmetic. Items on step-up in basis, estate tax thresholds, creditor priority, or required distributions for inherited retirement accounts have answers you cannot derive from first principles. As a screening test: if a numerate participant with no estate planning experience can reason to the answer, it is measuring numeracy.
  • Expand it. Three indicators is the identification minimum and leaves no room to detect problems. Eight to ten would make the EPL-Fin dimension testable rather than fragile.
  • Keep the legal/administrative items. They are the strongest part of the instrument: lowest correlation with FL (0.63), the strongest association with EP engagement net of financial literacy (Section 8.2), and content that genuinely requires knowing a legal default rather than computing one.
  • Design in a discriminant criterion. Recruit a known-groups sample — people who have completed estate planning, or professionals — and check that EPL separates them while FL does not. That is a stronger test of the construct than any factor model.
  • Consider separating knowledge from confidence. Treating blanks as wrong conflates “does not know” with “knows and is wrong.” Capturing confidence alongside each answer would let you model them separately.
